question:
HNO₃ (aq) + KOH(aq) → KNO₃ (aq) + H₂O (1)

The above reaction is an example of:
solution:
The correct answer is __**neutralisation reaction**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The reaction between HNO3 (aq) and KOH (aq) to form KNO3 (aq) and H2O (l) is an example of a **neutralisation reaction**.
 
• In a neutralisation reaction, **an acid reacts with a base to produce a salt and water**.
 
• Here, nitric acid (HNO3) neutralises potassium hydroxide (KOH) to form potassium nitrate (KNO3) and water (H2O).
 
• Neutralisation reactions are a type of double displacement reaction where the hydrogen ions from the acid react with the hydroxide ions from the base to form water.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Redox reactions** involve the **transfer of electrons** between two species. In this case, there is no transfer of electrons, so it is not a redox reaction.
 
• **Decomposition reactions** involve a single compound **breaking down into two or more simpler substances**. The given reaction does not fit this description.
 
• **Combination reactions** involve **two or more substances combining** to form a single product. The given reaction does not fit this description either.
 
• Neutralisation reactions are important in various industrial and laboratory processes, including titration methods used to determine the concentration of an unknown acid or base.
